findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build pipes whatever bytes the remote URL serves directly into a root shell. A compromised or changed upstream response can execute arbitrary build-time code and produces non-reproducible images.

findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer
findings.whyItBreaks: Building the image fetches and executes whatever bytes this URL (or a redirect target) returns. A compromised endpoint, DNS/transport interception, or changed script becomes arbitrary code execution in the build pipeline and produces a non-reproducible image.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every build fetches and executes whatever bytes the mutable URL serves at that moment. A compromised origin, DNS/TLS interception, or later script update runs arbitrary code in the image build and can silently change production artifacts.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key status in the exported helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding ErrMissing makes LoadOrDefault return the same empty string for an absent key and for a key explicitly stored with an empty value. As an exported API, every caller is forced to treat lookup failure as legitimate data and cannot safely decide whether to initialize, persist, or reject the value.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "", making absence indistinguishable from a present key whose value is legitimately empty. Callers are forced to treat failed loads as real data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal in the exported wrapper
findings.whyItBreaks: Discarding ErrMissing makes a missing key return the same "" value as a present key whose value is empty. Because LoadOrDefault is exported, callers cannot distinguish absence from legitimate stored data.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run returned only after every value had been delivered to results. It now launches sends asynchronously and returns immediately. A caller that closes results or treats Run's return as completion can race with these goroutines, causing sends on a closed channel or missing results.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every value had been sent. It now launches senders and returns immediately. A caller that closes results after Run returns (valid under the prior behavior) can race with these goroutines and panic with "send on closed channel"; blocked sends can also leak goroutines.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run did not return until every result had been sent. It now only launches goroutines, so callers may close results immediately after Run returns; any scheduled sender then panics with "send on closed channel". Callers also can no longer rely on Run completion to mean all jobs were processed.

findings.title: Require admin status before allowing record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true when session.isAdmin is false but session.tenantId matches the record. This grants every ordinary user in a tenant permission to delete any tenant record, including records they do not own.

findings.title: Require both admin status and tenant ownership
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || grants deletion when either condition holds: any non-admin user can delete records in their own tenant, and an admin can delete records belonging to another tenant. The prior predicate required both authorization boundaries.

findings.title: Require admin and tenant match for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: With isAdmin=false and session.tenantId equal to record.tenantId, the new expression evaluates true. This bypasses the prior admin requirement and authorizes non-admin users to delete records.

findings.title: Preserve valid settings instead of overwriting them after parse failure
findings.whyItBreaks: A partially invalid saved value such as {"theme":"dark"} previously throws, so updateFontSize does not save. It now becomes DEFAULTS, and updateFontSize saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}, permanently replacing the user's valid dark theme.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch conflates malformed or schema-invalid input with valid defaults. updateFontSize then receives that fallback and saves it at lines 20-22, replacing the user's unreadable settings with {"theme":"light","fontSize":size}; previously the parse error prevented this destructive write.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting stored settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch converts malformed or schema-invalid stored settings into defaults. updateFontSize then treats that fallback as valid and saves it, replacing the user's existing settings with `{ theme: "light", fontSize: <new size> }`; previously the parse error prevented this destructive write.

findings.whyItBreaks: Math.floor drops any remainder. For example, pageCount(11, 10) now returns 1 even though two pages are required to expose all 11 items.

findings.title: Use the requested commit when loading report artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: For buildReport(build, branch), builtFrom remains build.ref(branch), but artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). When those refs differ, the returned report falsely associates verified's artifacts with the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom contains build.ref(branch) but artifacts are fetched from build.ref("verified"). The returned report therefore associates one commit with another commit's artifacts.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported branch
findings.whyItBreaks: When `branch` and `verified` resolve to different commits, `builtFrom` reports `build.ref(branch)` while `artifacts` are fetched from `build.ref("verified")`. Consumers receive a self-inconsistent report and can attribute verified artifacts to the wrong branch commit.

findings.title: Honor the supplied entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this now returns all reversed entries instead of at most `limit`. For example, `renderFeed` passes 20 at line 9; with 21 inputs it writes index 20 into a 20-slot array, expanding the rendered feed to 21 entries.

findings.title: Respect limit before returning the feed
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most limit entries. renderFeed calls it with 20 at src/feed.ts:9; when all has more than 20 entries, its loop extends the initially 20-slot array and returns more than 20 feed entries.

findings.title: Apply the positive limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most `limit`. Consequently, `renderFeed` requests 20 entries at line 9 but its loop copies the full page, expanding the 20-element output array whenever `all` has more than 20 entries.

findings.title: Count only emitted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: With one live and one stale entry, this emits `# entry-count: 2` but only one data row. Consumers that use the header to determine the number of rows will over-read or reject the manifest.

findings.title: Keep header count aligned with emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries removes their rows, but the header still receives entries.length. A manifest with stale entries advertises more entries than it contains, which can cause consumers that validate or preallocate from # entry-count to reject or misread it.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is omitted but `headerLines` still receives `entries.length`, so `# entry-count` claims more entries than the manifest contains. Consumers using that header to validate or preallocate for the listed rows will receive invalid manifest metadata.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: FormatLegacyID is an exported Go package API. Removing it makes any existing consumer that formats persisted or interoperating LEG identifiers fail to compile on upgrade, with no replacement or migration path.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Deleting exported FormatLegacyID is a source-breaking API change: any downstream consumer calling ids.FormatLegacyID no longer compiles and loses the LEG-prefixed identifier format.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was a public export of src/orders.ts and is removed by this change. Existing consumers importing it from this module will fail to compile or load after upgrading, while the replacement quoteShipping is exported only from a new module path.

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of throwing unconditionally
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but every invocation now throws "always fails"; callers cannot obtain the previously implemented uppercase result.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every valid call to the exported execute(input: string): string API now throws "always fails" rather than returning a string, breaking its public result contract.

findings.title: Restore successful execution for valid input
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is the repository's only exported function and previously returned input.toUpperCase(). This change makes every invocation throw "always fails", so no valid input can produce a string result.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, this new guard returns false, so handle() returns "rejected" at line 24. Before this change, the same request passed eligibility and returned "read-only"; the explicit viewer branch at line 25 is now unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only outcome
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously passed isEligible and handle returned "read-only". The new role check rejects that same request before handle reaches its viewer branch, so viewers receive "rejected" instead.

findings.title: Keep active viewers eligible for read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit previously reached handle's "read-only" branch, but now isEligible returns false and handle returns "rejected" instead. The role-specific branch at line 25 establishes that viewers are a supported read-only action, not an ineligible request.

findings.title: Do not require payment to save a draft
findings.whyItBreaks: An order with state="draft" and payment="missing" could be saved before this change, but canProceed now returns false and saveDraft returns "blocked". Payment is relevant to submitting an order, not to persisting an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Keep payment gating out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: Adding `payment === "paid"` to the shared `canProceed` predicate makes `saveDraft` return "blocked" for an unpaid draft. Saving a draft is distinct from submitting an order and must remain available before payment.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from `stable`, the returned `commit` identifies that channel's head while `files` are read from `stable`. Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish or inspect the wrong file set.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit identifies that channel's head while Snapshot.files contains stable's files. Consumers publishing or inspecting the snapshot therefore receive mismatched commit metadata and content.

findings.title: Load snapshot files from the declared commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The snapshot declares commit as the requested channel's head, but files are read from the unrelated stable head. When those refs differ, consumers receive a self-inconsistent snapshot and may publish or inspect files that do not belong to snapshot.commit.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling `build(prefix, limit=3)` still returns 10 items because the implementation continues to iterate over the hard-coded `max_count = 10`. The public parameter therefore promises a caller-observable cap that is not implemented.

findings.title: Honor the public limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `limit` promises a caller-controlled output bound, but the body still unconditionally sets `max_count = 10`; for example, `build("x", limit=3)` returns 10 entries rather than 3.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=1) still returns ten items because the loop reads the hard-coded max_count=10 rather than limit. Callers cannot obtain the result cap exposed by the public signature.

findings.title: Validate positive integers in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1, despite its public name promising a positive result; charge('-1') consequently returns -100.

findings.title: Validate that parsed integers are positive
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1 and charge('-1') returns -100, contradicting the public function's positive-value contract.

findings.title: Validate that parse_positive_int returns a positive value
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` promises a positive integer but delegates directly to `int`, which accepts `0` and negative values. `charge('-1')` therefore returns `-100`, exposing a result that violates the new public contract.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame's immutability
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, apply_values copied df and returned the modified copy. It now writes through to df and returns the same object, so callers that retain df for later use will observe their source data unexpectedly changed.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously apply_values made a defensive copy and returned the modified copy. It now writes through to df, so callers that retain df for later use silently observe the mapped values rather than the original data.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mappings
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation copied df and updated the copy. This version updates df directly, so callers that retain the original DataFrame for later comparison, retry, or alternate transformations will observe it unexpectedly modified.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-value contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-2")` returns `-2` (and `"0"` returns `0`), contradicting its public contract; `charge("-2")` consequently produces `-200`.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1` and `parse_positive_int("0")` returns `0`, contradicting its public name. Its caller then converts `"-1"` into a `-100` charge at src/parse.rs:6-7.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but `"-1"` returns -1 and `"0"` returns 0. Callers such as `charge` therefore produce negative or zero charges while relying on a parser whose advertised contract says that cannot happen.

findings.title: Avoid moving items before computing its length
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value, producing Rust error E0382 and blocking builds.

findings.title: Remove the debug macro that consumes `items`
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` evaluates and drops its returned `Vec<String>`, moving `items`; the subsequent `items.len()` therefore fails with a use-after-move compile error.

findings.title: Borrow `items` when logging it
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` takes ownership of the `Vec<String>`; the subsequent `items.len()` then borrows a moved value, producing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: `fromRevision` remains the pinned tag revision, but `changedPaths` is now computed from `latest`. Consumers replay paths on `fromRevision` per the exported Changeset contract, so the paths can describe a different tree and cause incorrect or failed replays whenever the pinned tag differs from latest.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: For any pinnedTag that does not resolve to "latest", the returned fromRevision is `from` while changedPaths is computed from `latest`. Consumers are documented to replay changedPaths on fromRevision, so they receive a changeset relative to the wrong base and can omit or apply the wrong paths.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the returned base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: fromRevision remains the revision resolved from pinnedTag, but changedPaths are now read using the separately resolved latest revision. This violates the exported Changeset contract that consumers replay paths on exactly fromRevision; when pinnedTag is behind latest, consumers receive a path set for the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration removes users.email, src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users, which fails because email no longer exists.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still runs `SELECT email FROM users`, which fails with a missing-column error on upgraded databases.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; that query will fail with a missing-column error after upgrade.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: The literal bk_live_... credential is embedded in source, exposing billing API access to every repository reader and any distributed build artifact. It also ignores BILLING_API_KEY, so deployments cannot select their own billing account.

findings.title: Restore environment-backed billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The bk_live credential is committed to version control, exposing production billing access to every repository reader and artifact consumer. makeClient now also ignores BILLING_API_KEY, preventing normal per-environment configuration and credential rotation.

findings.title: Restore environment-based billing credential validation
findings.whyItBreaks: This embeds a `bk_live_` credential in source, exposing it to everyone with repository access and making every deployment use the same production billing identity. It also changes a missing BILLING_API_KEY from an explicit startup failure into apparent success, so misconfigured deployments can send billing traffic with the committed credential.

findings.title: Restore the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The changed startup path now immediately indexes None, raising TypeError instead of starting with the prior default of one worker.

findings.title: Preserve defaults when the settings file is absent
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7). startup now immediately subscripts that None value, raising TypeError instead of returning the previous default worker count of 1.

findings.title: Restore handling for a missing settings file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() returns None when path does not exist, and startup() now immediately indexes settings["workers"]. A missing config file therefore raises TypeError rather than starting with the previous default of one worker.

findings.title: Propagate gateway failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error and returns nil. Callers of this exported API therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a successful one and may continue processing it as paid.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a successful one and may treat an uncollected payment as completed. Charge is exported, so this broken error contract affects external callers even though there are no in-repository call sites.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, Charge logs it and then returns nil at line 19. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed payment from a completed charge and may continue or record it as successful.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches "theme", a request for tenant B's "theme" uses the identical `settings:theme` key and returns A's cached value at line 14 without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, "theme")`. This regresses the prior `${tenantId}:${name}` partitioning and can apply one tenant's configuration to another.

findings.title: Keep tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A reads a setting such as `apiKey`, it is stored under `settings:apiKey`. A later `settingsFor('tenant-b', 'apiKey', store)` call hits that entry at line 13 and returns tenant A's value without calling the tenant-scoped `SettingsStore.fetch(tenantId, name)` method. This leaks tenant-specific settings and also serves stale/wrong configuration.

findings.title: Keep cached settings scoped to their tenant
findings.whyItBreaks: The cache key now contains only name. After settingsFor("tenant-a", "theme", store) caches tenant-a's value, settingsFor("tenant-b", "theme", store) returns that cached value without calling store.fetch, leaking or misapplying tenant-a's setting.

findings.title: Preserve tenant-aware invalidation compatibility
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported function changed from invalidate(tenantId, name) to invalidate(name). Existing TypeScript consumers no longer compile; existing JavaScript consumers calling invalidate(tenantId, name) delete settings:<tenantId> instead of the requested setting entry, leaving stale cached data.

findings.title: Serialize reservations across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls can both read remaining=1 before either save resolves, both persist 0, and both return true. This records two successful reservations for one unit.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields after reading stock but before updating it. Two concurrent reserve calls with stock=1 both read 1, both save 0, and both return true, so one unit can be reserved twice.

findings.title: Preserve Inventory's public construction and reserve APIs
findings.whyItBreaks: Inventory is exported, but existing consumers using new Inventory() now fail to type-check because Store is required. Existing synchronous callers also receive Promise<boolean> instead of boolean, changing conditions such as if (inventory.reserve(sku)) to take the truthy Promise path without waiting for persistence.

findings.title: Make reservation atomic across the persistence await
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent reserve("sku") calls can both read the same positive remaining value before either await completes, both persist the same decremented count, and both return true. Previously the synchronous stock update caused the second call to return false.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Inventory public API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers using new Inventory() no longer type-check (and JavaScript consumers will later dereference an undefined store). Existing synchronous callers also receive a Promise instead of a boolean, so `if (inventory.reserve(sku))` becomes truthy even when stock is empty.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1,000 before sleeping. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (16m40s) instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30 minutes instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Update retry to consume the millisecond backoff value
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies its result by 1000. A first failed retry waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16m 40s) instead of 1,000 ms, and capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (about 8h 20m).

findings.title: Remove the stale seconds-to-milliseconds conversion in retry
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to sleep(). The first retry waits 1,000,000 ms (~16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second; capped retries wait 30,000,000 ms (~8.3 hours) instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: When w.Flush succeeds but f.Close fails, deferred f.Close() ignores that error and Save returns nil. Callers of this exported API can therefore treat an unsuccessfully finalized write as saved.

findings.title: Propagate the deferred file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: On the successful write path, Save now returns only w.Flush() and ignores f.Close() via defer. Close can report a final filesystem error, so callers can receive nil even though the file was not durably completed. The previous implementation returned that error.

findings.title: Propagate the file close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred Close return value is discarded. Previously, after a successful Flush, Save returned f.Close()'s error. A close can surface delayed filesystem failures, so callers can now receive nil even though the save did not complete successfully.

findings.title: Include the page’s final row
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is exclusive, but `range(start, end - 1)` stops one element early. For example, a two-row page returns only its first row; a final one-row page returns no rows. `render_page` and `summarize` therefore silently omit data.

findings.title: Include the final row in each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds helper defines end as exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) excludes the item at end - 1. Consequently every nonempty page loses its last row; page_size=1 produces empty pages, and summarize/render_page silently omit rows.

findings.title: Include the end element when collecting a page
findings.whyItBreaks: The documented half-open bounds make end exclusive, but range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1 as well. Every nonempty page loses its final row; a one-row page renders empty, and summarize silently omits those rows.

findings.title: Return cache entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age near zero, so with a positive TTL the new `>` condition deletes it and returns null. Once expired, it instead returns the stale value indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove all completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next job left while `forEach` advances its index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job is skipped and remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return cache entries while they remain within TTL
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove completed jobs without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during `forEach` shifts the next job into the current index, but `forEach` then advances to the following index. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison is inverted: fresh entries are deleted and return null, while entries older than ttlMs are returned as valid cache hits.

findings.title: Avoid splicing while iterating forward
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but forEach advances to the next index. Adjacent completed jobs are therefore skipped and remain in the returned queue.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result for averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: For rows=[], reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN instead of the prior numeric result 0. Callers of this exported function can no longer safely use its result as an amount.

findings.title: Do not reorder the input array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows. The previous implementation explicitly sorted a copied array, so callers could retain their original ordering; this change silently reorders caller-owned data.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average of zero
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty array, reduce returns 0 and rows.length is 0, so this returns NaN. The previous implementation returned 0, making empty input distinguishable as a valid zero average.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates `rows`. Previously, busiest() sorted a copy, so callers could reuse their input order after selecting the busiest row. This change silently reorders that caller-owned data.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input average
findings.whyItBreaks: For an empty Row[] the reduction is 0 and rows.length is 0, so this now returns NaN instead of the prior documented-by-behavior value 0. Callers receiving a number can propagate NaN into totals or displays.

findings.title: Do not reorder the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates rows in place. The previous implementation explicitly sorted a copy, so callers that reuse rows after calling busiest() now observe their original ordering silently changed.

findings.title: Restore numeric score comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For scores [9, 100, 80] and n=1, rankScores returns [9, 80, 100], so cutoff becomes 9 and topPlayers returns the first input player (score 9) instead of the player with score 100.
